screens.title: Enhanced Input System — concepts and benefits
screens.narratorSegment: The Enhanced Input System abstracts what the player wants to do from the physical control used to do it. An Input Action represents an intent like Jump, Move, or Interact. An Input Mapping Context (IMC) groups those actions and maps them to keys, mouse buttons, or gamepad axes. The key benefit is mode-awareness: you can activate a gameplay IMC while the player is on foot and swap to a vehicle IMC when they enter a car, preventing unintended actions. A concrete example: define a Jump Input Action and map Spacebar in a Player_IMC. If the player opens a menu, remove the Player_IMC and add a UI_IMC, so joystick movement no longer moves the character while navigating menus. A common misconception is that Enhanced Input is just a rebinding tool; it also provides lifecycle events like OnInputStarted and gives better context stacking. Misusing contexts by leaving an old context active can cause conflicting inputs — always explicitly add and remove IMCs on state changes. Takeaway: think of Input Actions as verbs and IMCs as mode-specific keyrings that you hang on or take off depending on gameplay state. Which action would you make context-aware first?

keyIdea.title: Enhanced Input
keyIdea.text: Use Input Actions for intent, IMCs for mode-specific mappings, and add/remove contexts to avoid input conflicts.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Enhanced Input
Definition & core claim

An Input Action models a player intent; an Input Mapping Context binds that intent to physical inputs for a gameplay mode.

Benefits
  • Mode-specific mappings prevent accidental actions.
  • Supports remapping without changing gameplay code.
  • Provides lifecycle events for richer input handling.
Example
Map a Jump Input Action to Spacebar in Player_IMC. When a menu opens, remove Player_IMC and add UI_IMC so movement input is ignored while the UI is active.
Common mistake
Leaving multiple conflicting IMCs active produces duplicate or unintended responses. Always manage context lifecycle explicitly when changing gameplay modes.
Pro tip
Use priority ordering and remove obsolete contexts immediately after mode change to avoid stacking issues.
Key Takeaway

Treat Input Actions as verbs and IMCs as mode keyrings; add and remove contexts to keep behavior predictable.

screens.title: Activating and switching Input Mapping Contexts
screens.narratorSegment: Switching Input Mapping Contexts is a simple but powerful pattern for mode-specific control. The flow: determine when a mode change occurs, add the new context to the player's Enhanced Input Local Player Subsystem, and remove the old context. A concrete example: when the player enters a vehicle trigger, call Add Input Mapping Context with IMC_Player_Vehicle and Remove Input Mapping Context for IMC_Player_OnFoot. This prevents on-foot movement code from running while driving. Common pitfalls include forgetting to remove the previous context or adding contexts with overlapping actions without explicit priority, which can create duplicate triggers. Testing strategy: instrument the mode change event with print statements and verify that input behavior changes as expected. For remapping support, keep Input Actions stable and only swap contexts. Another misconception is attempting to bind physical keys at runtime instead of using IMCs; prefer context switching to preserve abstraction and remapping. Takeaway: always treat IMC swaps as explicit state transitions and verify them during playtesting so controls remain deterministic. Activating and switching Input Mapping Contexts means add and remove imcs at mode boundaries to ensure only relevant actions are active and avoid conflicting inputs.. In practical terms, how to add and remove contexts when modes change. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Switching IMCs
Mode change steps
  1. Detect mode trigger (enter vehicle, open menu).
  2. Call Add Input Mapping Context for the new IMC.
  3. Call Remove Input Mapping Context for the old IMC.
  4. Optionally set priority or consume input events.
Example
On vehicle entry: Add IMC_Player_Vehicle, Remove IMC_Player_OnFoot. On exit, reverse the calls.
Checklist
  • Are old contexts removed? If not, remove them explicitly.
  • Do IMCs share actions that need priority? Assign ordering.
  • Are remaps preserved? Keep Input Actions stable across contexts.
Key Takeaway

Treat context swaps as explicit state transitions and verify them during testing to avoid conflicting behavior.

screens.title: Input Action vs Axis Mapping
screens.narratorSegment: Input Actions represent discrete or structured player intents, while axis mappings typically provide continuous values used for movement or aiming. In the Enhanced Input System you model both as Input Actions: an action can carry a value or be triggered. For movement, your Move action will often carry two-dimensional values from a joystick or WASD and feed into Add Movement Input with a direction vector and the action's scale. A common example: a Move Input Action mapped to the left stick returns an X and Y axis pair that you interpret relative to the camera to call Add Movement Input along forward and right vectors. A misconception is to treat Input Actions only as button presses; they can carry analog data and be sampled continuously. Another mistake is applying raw axis values without normalizing by frame time or character speed controls, which leads to inconsistent movement across frame rates. The practical takeaway: design Input Actions to match the semantic intent you need — discrete events for Interact, analog values for movement — and convert values into world-space movement via the Character Movement Component so physics and collisions remain correct. How will you map your Move action for camera-relative control?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Actions vs Axes
Concept

Treat discrete intents like Interact as triggers. Treat continuous controls like Move as analog inputs that supply values to movement systems.

Concrete example
A Move Input Action returns an X/Y vector. Multiply that vector by camera forward/right to produce world movement vectors, then call Add Movement Input with those directions and the appropriate scale.
Common mistake
Feeding raw axis values directly into position updates bypasses the Character Movement Component and its collision handling. Use Add Movement Input to keep physics consistent.
Key Takeaway

Map analog actions to movement vectors and always route movement through the Character Movement Component for correct physics and collisions.

screens.title: Character movement wiring
screens.narratorSegment: Character movement in Blueprints typically uses Add Movement Input and relies on the Character Movement Component to handle physics and collisions. The pattern: sample your Move Input Action values, compute world-space forward and right directions from the camera or control rotation, and call Add Movement Input with those direction vectors and the action values as scale. A concrete example: when the Move action returns a Y value of 1 and X value of 0, compute Forward = Get Control Rotation forward vector and call Add Movement Input(Forward, 1.0). A misconception is to set actor location directly from input axes; this bypasses collision and slope handling. Another issue is forgetting to multiply by delta time in custom velocity calculations—Add Movement Input handles frame scaling with movement component settings. Testing: use the default Character Movement Component settings first, then tweak Max Walk Speed and gravity. The closing question: how will you convert camera-relative input into movement for a platformer versus a top-down game? Consider which direction vectors to use. Character movement wiring means sample input, compute world directions, and call add movement input to let character movement component manage motion and collisions.. In practical terms, using add movement input and the character movement component. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Character Movement
Blueprint pattern
[Sample logic]
Get Input Action "Move" -> Get Value (X,Y)
Get Control Rotation -> Get Forward Vector, Get Right Vector
Add Movement Input(Forward, Value.Y)
Add Movement Input(Right, Value.X)
This keeps movement consistent with the Character Movement Component and leverages existing physics and collision responses.
Example scenario
On a slope the Character Movement Component will handle sliding and step-up, which you preserve by using Add Movement Input instead of directly setting locations.
Key Takeaway

Route motion through Add Movement Input and tune the Character Movement Component for desired behaviors.

screens.title: Traces for interaction detection
screens.narratorSegment: Traces are your primary method for detecting what the player is targeting without physical overlap. A Line Trace casts a ray from a start to an end point and returns the first blocking hit; a Sphere Trace casts a swept sphere and is more forgiving for small target windows. Typical pattern: perform a Line Trace starting at the player's camera or eye position and extending forward by an InteractionDistance (for example 500 units). Break Hit Result and check Hit Actor for an Interactable interface or a tag. Always verify the Trace Channel; if walls do not block the chosen channel the trace will pass through them and allow interactions through geometry. Debugging tip: enable Draw Debug Type: For Duration during development to see the trace in the viewport. A common misconception is that traces automatically ignore the player; you often need to set an ignore actor or adjust trace parameters to avoid hitting the player's own collision. Takeaway: pick the right trace type for the interaction and confirm collision responses for your world geometry before relying on traces in gameplay.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Traces
Trace types
  • Line Trace: precise, returns first blocking hit.
  • Sphere Trace: radius-based, better for slightly off-center targets.
Example
Start = Camera Location, End = Start + ForwardVector * InteractionDistance. Break Hit Result and test for interface implementation or tag.
Debug checklist
  • Is Trace Channel set to Visibility or a custom channel blocked by walls?
  • Are you ignoring the player actor to avoid self-hits?
  • Use Draw Debug Type to visualize the trace during testing.

Pick the trace that matches your interaction tolerance and confirm collision responses so traces hit what you expect.

screens.title: Implementing the BP_InteractableDoor
screens.narratorSegment: Building a simple door uses a timeline to animate movement and an interface to accept interactions from many object types. Steps: create BP_InteractableDoor as an Actor, add a Static Mesh for the door and a Box Collision for the trigger, and add a Timeline named DoorTimeline with a Float Track OpenAlpha keyed from 0 to 1 over one second. Implement BPI_Interactable with an Interact function, then in the Interact event call Play From Start on DoorTimeline. On the Timeline Update, Lerp between the initial relative location and the open location using OpenAlpha and Set Relative Location on the mesh. When Timeline Finished fires, connect to a Delay (for example 3 seconds) then call Reverse From End to close. Example scenario: the player traces a door and calls Interact; the door opens and closes after the delay. A common mistake is storing the open location as an absolute world location rather than relative, which causes issues when the door is moved in the editor. Always compute local offsets and store the mesh's initial relative transform at BeginPlay. What will you choose as the open offset for your door?

keyIdea.title: Door pattern
keyIdea.text: Use a Timeline output to drive a Lerp on the mesh transform, trigger Play From Start from Interact, and Reverse From End after a delay to close.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › BP_InteractableDoor
Blueprint steps
[BP_InteractableDoor Event Graph]
Event Interact (from BPI_Interactable)
  -> Play From Start (DoorTimeline)

DoorTimeline Update
  -> Lerp (Vector) (A: InitialLocation, B: InitialLocation + Z(200), Alpha: OpenAlpha)
  -> Set Relative Location (Static Mesh)

DoorTimeline Finished
  -> Delay (3.0)
  -> Reverse From End (DoorTimeline)
Remember to cache InitialLocation at BeginPlay so Lerp uses relative values and the door moves correctly if the actor is placed elsewhere in the level.
Example behavior
Player triggers Interact, door plays open timeline, remains open for three seconds, then reverses the timeline to close.
Common mistake
Using world locations instead of relative transforms causes misplacement when actors move or are instanced. Cache the mesh's relative transform at BeginPlay.
Key Takeaway

Timelines provide smooth, reversible animations; drive transforms with relative values and trigger playback from Interact events.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Trace → Interact
Event graph pattern
[BP_PlayerCharacter Event Graph]
Input Action Interact (Triggered)
  -> Line Trace By Channel
     Start: Camera Location
     End: Start + ForwardVector * 500
     Trace Channel: Visibility
  -> Break Hit Result
  -> Branch (Condition: Blocking Hit)
     True -> Does Implement Interface (BPI_Interactable) (Target: Hit Actor)
       -> Branch (Return Value)
          True -> Interact (Message) (Target: Hit Actor)
Include the player in Ignore Actors to avoid hits on self, and set Draw Debug Type to visualize traces while testing.
Example
Player presses Interact, the trace hits a door, Does Implement Interface returns true, and the door receives the Interact message to begin opening.
Common mistake
Using the wrong Trace Channel or not setting collision presets so walls block the chosen channel. Always verify collision settings for interactive props and geometry.
Key Takeaway

A trace + interface call pattern decouples the player from specific object types and keeps interaction logic modular and testable.

screens.title: Event-driven Blueprints and Interfaces
screens.narratorSegment: Event-driven programming changes the flow from polling to reacting. Instead of every actor checking conditions each tick, actors emit events and listeners respond. In Blueprints this is implemented with built-in events like OnComponentBeginOverlap and custom events or Blueprint Interfaces. The BPI_Interactable interface defines an Interact function that any actor can implement; when your trace hits an actor, you call Interact via the interface which invokes the actor's implementation without casting. Example: both BP_InteractableDoor and BP_Collectible implement BPI_Interactable. When the player calls Interact through the interface, the door plays its timeline and the collectible adds to inventory. A typical misconception is overusing casting to concrete types; interfaces let different objects respond polymorphically. Also avoid firing events that assume listeners exist; design events with optional handlers and safe defaults. The practical benefit is decoupling: you can add new interactable object types without changing player code. Which actor in your level could benefit from implementing Interact? Events let systems react only when something happens. This creates responsive and efficient Blueprints that are easier to debug.

screens.title: Common mistakes and debugging practices
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson consolidates common mistakes and how to debug them. First, traces passing through walls usually indicate the chosen Trace Channel isn't blocked by the wall's collision preset; check Project Settings → Collision and ensure your mesh presets block that channel. Second, context leaks happen when an IMC isn't removed on mode change; verify Add/Remove calls and instrument the swap with print statements. Third, timelines misbehave when you use absolute world transforms instead of relative mesh offsets; cache the initial relative location at BeginPlay and Lerp to an offset. Debugging techniques: enable Draw Debug Type: For Duration on trace nodes to see the ray or sphere, add Print String nodes to log hit actor names and hit distances, and temporarily change mesh collision to an obvious color or physics preset while testing. A misconception is believing performance is the main cause of missed traces; often it's collision setup. Final reflection: which debug technique will you include in your development habit to reduce iteration time? screens.title: Build the simple door interaction (activity)
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks you through creating the door interaction described earlier. Step 1: Create BP_InteractableDoor actor, add a Static Mesh and a Box Collision. Step 2: Add a Timeline named DoorTimeline and create a Float Track OpenAlpha from 0 at time 0 to 1 at time 1. Step 3: Create a Blueprint Interface BPI_Interactable with a function Interact and implement it in the door blueprint. Step 4: In the Interact event, call Play From Start on the timeline. On the timeline Update, Lerp between InitialLocation and InitialLocation + Z(200) and Set Relative Location on the Static Mesh. On Finished, add a Delay of 3 seconds then Reverse From End. Step 5: In your player character, add an Input Action Interact and on Triggered perform a Line Trace By Channel from the camera, break the hit, check Does Implement Interface, and call Interact if true. Test with Draw Debug Type enabled, and verify collision channels so the trace cannot go through walls. If you see unexpected hits, use Print String to inspect hit actor names. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn how to give players responsive control and meaningful ways to interact with the world. We start with the Enhanced Input System, which separates abstract actions from physical keys and lets you switch mapping contexts when gameplay mode changes. From there we'll translate input into character motion using the Character Movement Component and Add Movement Input, detect interactable objects with traces, and build a simple door that opens and closes using a timeline and an interactable interface. You will also see how GameMode and GameState coordinate global flow, how to pause and resume safely, and why event-driven Blueprint patterns and interfaces keep systems modular. Each section includes concrete Blueprints, a small hands-on activity, and common debugging tips such as using debug draw for traces or verifying collision responses. By the end you'll be able to wire input, implement a robust interaction pattern, and design game flow that is easier to test and extend. Which interaction will you implement first in your project?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to map player intent to reliable in-game actions, build a modular interaction pattern, manage basic game states, and use event-driven Blueprints to keep systems decoupled. First, you will learn to define Input Actions and populate an Input Mapping Context so that actions like Jump, Move, and Interact are abstracted from physical keys and can be remapped or swapped when gameplay mode changes. Second, you'll implement a detection and interaction pattern using traces and an Interactable interface so different objects can respond to the same call without direct casting. Third, you will manage game flow through GameMode and GameState, including safe pause handling and initialization steps. Fourth, you'll use events and Blueprint Interfaces to dispatch messages across actors, which prevents tight coupling and simplifies debugging. Each objective includes a concrete example and a mnemonic visual to help memory: think of contexts as mode-specific keyrings, traces as flashlight rays, GameMode as the rulebook, and interfaces as contracts. These skills matter because they reduce bugs, make systems extensible, and improve player control. Which objective will you practice first?

This continuation highlights practical checks you will perform and common issues to look for. You will learn to verify trace collision channels and object collision presets so traces do not pass through walls, and to choose appropriate trace types — a Line Trace for precise targeting or a Sphere Trace for forgiving detection. You will practice wiring a door timeline and learn the playback pattern: Play From Start when interacting, wait via a delay, then Reverse From End to close. You will also practice adding and removing Input Mapping Contexts when changing control modes, such as swapping to vehicle controls while driving. Finally, you will adopt debugging habits: enable Draw Debug for traces to visualize hits, log helpful messages in Blueprint during development, and check collision presets for interactable actors. These steps reduce common bugs and make testing repeatable. Which debugging habit will you add to your workflow first?

The Enhanced Input System abstracts what the player wants to do from the physical control used to do it. An Input Action represents an intent like Jump, Move, or Interact. An Input Mapping Context (IMC) groups those actions and maps them to keys, mouse buttons, or gamepad axes. The key benefit is mode-awareness: you can activate a gameplay IMC while the player is on foot and swap to a vehicle IMC when they enter a car, preventing unintended actions. A concrete example: define a Jump Input Action and map Spacebar in a Player_IMC. If the player opens a menu, remove the Player_IMC and add a UI_IMC, so joystick movement no longer moves the character while navigating menus. A common misconception is that Enhanced Input is just a rebinding tool; it also provides lifecycle events like OnInputStarted and gives better context stacking. Misusing contexts by leaving an old context active can cause conflicting inputs — always explicitly add and remove IMCs on state changes. Takeaway: think of Input Actions as verbs and IMCs as mode-specific keyrings that you hang on or take off depending on gameplay state. Which action would you make context-aware first?

Switching Input Mapping Contexts is a simple but powerful pattern for mode-specific control. The flow: determine when a mode change occurs, add the new context to the player's Enhanced Input Local Player Subsystem, and remove the old context. A concrete example: when the player enters a vehicle trigger, call Add Input Mapping Context with IMC_Player_Vehicle and Remove Input Mapping Context for IMC_Player_OnFoot. This prevents on-foot movement code from running while driving. Common pitfalls include forgetting to remove the previous context or adding contexts with overlapping actions without explicit priority, which can create duplicate triggers. Testing strategy: instrument the mode change event with print statements and verify that input behavior changes as expected. For remapping support, keep Input Actions stable and only swap contexts. Another misconception is attempting to bind physical keys at runtime instead of using IMCs; prefer context switching to preserve abstraction and remapping. Takeaway: always treat IMC swaps as explicit state transitions and verify them during playtesting so controls remain deterministic. Activating and switching Input Mapping Contexts means add and remove imcs at mode boundaries to ensure only relevant actions are active and avoid conflicting inputs.. In practical terms, how to add and remove contexts when modes change. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Input Actions represent discrete or structured player intents, while axis mappings typically provide continuous values used for movement or aiming. In the Enhanced Input System you model both as Input Actions: an action can carry a value or be triggered. For movement, your Move action will often carry two-dimensional values from a joystick or WASD and feed into Add Movement Input with a direction vector and the action's scale. A common example: a Move Input Action mapped to the left stick returns an X and Y axis pair that you interpret relative to the camera to call Add Movement Input along forward and right vectors. A misconception is to treat Input Actions only as button presses; they can carry analog data and be sampled continuously. Another mistake is applying raw axis values without normalizing by frame time or character speed controls, which leads to inconsistent movement across frame rates. The practical takeaway: design Input Actions to match the semantic intent you need — discrete events for Interact, analog values for movement — and convert values into world-space movement via the Character Movement Component so physics and collisions remain correct. How will you map your Move action for camera-relative control?

Character movement in Blueprints typically uses Add Movement Input and relies on the Character Movement Component to handle physics and collisions. The pattern: sample your Move Input Action values, compute world-space forward and right directions from the camera or control rotation, and call Add Movement Input with those direction vectors and the action values as scale. A concrete example: when the Move action returns a Y value of 1 and X value of 0, compute Forward = Get Control Rotation forward vector and call Add Movement Input(Forward, 1.0). A misconception is to set actor location directly from input axes; this bypasses collision and slope handling. Another issue is forgetting to multiply by delta time in custom velocity calculations—Add Movement Input handles frame scaling with movement component settings. Testing: use the default Character Movement Component settings first, then tweak Max Walk Speed and gravity. The closing question: how will you convert camera-relative input into movement for a platformer versus a top-down game? Consider which direction vectors to use. Character movement wiring means sample input, compute world directions, and call add movement input to let character movement component manage motion and collisions.. In practical terms, using add movement input and the character movement component. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Traces are your primary method for detecting what the player is targeting without physical overlap. A Line Trace casts a ray from a start to an end point and returns the first blocking hit; a Sphere Trace casts a swept sphere and is more forgiving for small target windows. Typical pattern: perform a Line Trace starting at the player's camera or eye position and extending forward by an InteractionDistance (for example 500 units). Break Hit Result and check Hit Actor for an Interactable interface or a tag. Always verify the Trace Channel; if walls do not block the chosen channel the trace will pass through them and allow interactions through geometry. Debugging tip: enable Draw Debug Type: For Duration during development to see the trace in the viewport. A common misconception is that traces automatically ignore the player; you often need to set an ignore actor or adjust trace parameters to avoid hitting the player's own collision. Takeaway: pick the right trace type for the interaction and confirm collision responses for your world geometry before relying on traces in gameplay.

Building a simple door uses a timeline to animate movement and an interface to accept interactions from many object types. Steps: create BP_InteractableDoor as an Actor, add a Static Mesh for the door and a Box Collision for the trigger, and add a Timeline named DoorTimeline with a Float Track OpenAlpha keyed from 0 to 1 over one second. Implement BPI_Interactable with an Interact function, then in the Interact event call Play From Start on DoorTimeline. On the Timeline Update, Lerp between the initial relative location and the open location using OpenAlpha and Set Relative Location on the mesh. When Timeline Finished fires, connect to a Delay (for example 3 seconds) then call Reverse From End to close. Example scenario: the player traces a door and calls Interact; the door opens and closes after the delay. A common mistake is storing the open location as an absolute world location rather than relative, which causes issues when the door is moved in the editor. Always compute local offsets and store the mesh's initial relative transform at BeginPlay. What will you choose as the open offset for your door?

To let the player call Interact on objects, perform a trace from the player's viewpoint, check the hit, and dispatch the interface call. The typical chain: on Input Action Interact Triggered, perform Line Trace By Channel with Start = Get Actor Location or Camera Location and End = Start + ForwardVector * InteractionDistance (e. g., 500 units). Set Trace Channel to Visibility or a custom Interact channel. Break the Hit Result, branch on Blocking Hit, then call Does Implement Interface for BPI_Interactable on Hit Actor. If true, call Interact (Message) on Hit Actor. Concrete example: if you hit BP_InteractableDoor, Interact triggers Play From Start on its timeline and opens the door. A common bug is traces hitting unexpected components because collision presets are misconfigured. Fix by checking collision presets and ensuring walls block your chosen channel. Another pitfall is not ignoring the player actor; include the player in the Trace's Ignore Actors array to prevent self-hits. Final reflection: how would you adapt this to a sphere trace to allow a forgiving interaction cone? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

GameMode and GameState coordinate global rules and replicated state. GameMode defines the game rules: player spawning, starting match logic, and authoritative operations reserved to server-side contexts. GameState holds global information that should be visible to all clients, like time remaining or scores, and can be used in single-player to share persistent data across actors. A practical single-player example: implement a StartGame function in GameMode that initializes player score, spawns level-specific objectives, and sets the initial input mapping context. If you implement a Pause menu, call Set Game Paused true, show the UI widget, and disable player input by removing the gameplay IMC. Event-driven programming changes the flow from polling to reacting. Instead of every actor checking conditions each tick, actors emit events and listeners respond. In Blueprints this is implemented with built-in events like OnComponentBeginOverlap and custom events or Blueprint Interfaces. The BPI_Interactable interface defines an Interact function that any actor can implement; when your trace hits an actor, you call Interact via the interface which invokes the actor's implementation without casting. Example: both BP_InteractableDoor and BP_Collectible implement BPI_Interactable. When the player calls Interact through the interface, the door plays its timeline and the collectible adds to inventory. A typical misconception is overusing casting to concrete types; interfaces let different objects respond polymorphically. Also avoid firing events that assume listeners exist; design events with optional handlers and safe defaults. The practical benefit is decoupling: you can add new interactable object types without changing player code. Which actor in your level could benefit from implementing Interact? This lesson consolidates common mistakes and how to debug them. First, traces passing through walls usually indicate the chosen Trace Channel isn't blocked by the wall's collision preset; check Project Settings → Collision and ensure your mesh presets block that channel. Second, context leaks happen when an IMC isn't removed on mode change; verify Add/Remove calls and instrument the swap with print statements. Third, timelines misbehave when you use absolute world transforms instead of relative mesh offsets; cache the initial relative location at BeginPlay and Lerp to an offset. Debugging techniques: enable Draw Debug Type: For Duration on trace nodes to see the ray or sphere, add Print String nodes to log hit actor names and hit distances, and temporarily change mesh collision to an obvious color or physics preset while testing. A misconception is believing performance is the main cause of missed traces; often it's collision setup. This hands-on activity walks you through creating the door interaction described earlier. Step 1: Create BP_InteractableDoor actor, add a Static Mesh and a Box Collision. On the timeline Update, Lerp between InitialLocation and InitialLocation + Z(200) and Set Relative Location on the Static Mesh. On Finished, add a Delay of 3 seconds then Reverse From End. Here are the compact core concepts to carry forward. The Enhanced Input System decouples intents from physical keys using Input Actions and Input Mapping Contexts so controls can be swapped by mode. Use Add Movement Input with camera-relative directions to let the Character Movement Component manage physics and collision. Detect interactables with Line or Sphere Traces, and always validate your trace channel and collision presets if traces behave unpredictably. Implement Blueprint Interfaces like BPI_Interactable to call Interact on varied actors without casting. Use GameMode for authoritative rules and GameState for shared, observable data; manage pause by toggling input contexts and Set Game Paused. Finally, embrace event-driven design to reduce polling and tight coupling. Keep a short debug checklist: Draw Debug for traces, Print String for hit logs, and verify collision settings. To close, hold three reminders: one, always separate intent from inputs using actions and contexts so controls can be remapped and swapped per mode. Two, favor the Character Movement Component and Add Movement Input for motion so collision and physics remain consistent. Three, design interactions as messages via Blueprint Interfaces and use traces with correct channels; this prevents tight coupling and makes things simple to add or replace. When testing, enable trace debug draw, log hits, and confirm collision presets. These habits save time and reduce subtle bugs like interaction through walls or input leaks between modes.
